title: Overpaying Your Mortgage Always Wins? Savings Pay £442… Until the Tax Bill 🏠😱 #shorts
description:
Got £10,000 spare? At today's average rates a savings account can pay more than overpaying your mortgage saves, until tax takes its cut.

The numbers (Bank of England, September 2026 averages, published 29 October): the average rate on outstanding mortgages is 4.03%, so overpaying £10,000 saves roughly £403 of interest in the first year (about £400). The average rate on new fixed-term savings deals is 4.42%: £442 a year on £10,000.

The catch: savings interest is taxed once you've used your Personal Savings Allowance (£1,000 of interest a year for basic-rate taxpayers, £500 for higher rate). Budget 2026 raises the savings basic rate from 20% to 24% from 6 April 2027 (higher rate 40% to 44%). So a basic-rate saver who has used the allowance keeps £336 of the £442 from April 2027 (£353.60 at today's 20%); a higher-rate saver keeps £247.52 at 44%. Overpaying's saving isn't taxed, so it wins again. Interest inside an ISA stays tax-free.

One thing people miss: normal overpayments usually can't be taken back out (flexible and offset mortgages can), and many lenders only allow up to 10% a year without an early repayment charge. MoneyHelper suggests keeping enough savings for at least three months first.

Sources: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/statistics/money-and-credit/2026/september-2026 · https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/statistics/effective-interest-rates/2026/september-2026 · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/budget-2026-overview-of-tax-legislation-and-rates-ootlar/annex-a-rates-and-allowances · https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/income-tax-changes-to-tax-rates-for-property-and-savings-income/income-tax-changes-to-tax-rates-for-property-and-savings-income · https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/homes/buying-a-home/should-you-pay-off-your-mortgage-early
